ann_89.original: The direct edges form a linear score added to the output. The largest terms, per standard deviation of the input and through each input's own edge: voice mail plan -0.99, number of voicemail messages 0.51, Vermont -0.24, Hawaii -0.17, international charge 0.16, Washington 0.14 and day charge 0.13. The direct customer-service-call edge is small (-0.09): the service-call effect comes through the gates in serviceIntlUsageCore. Self-probe on the typical customer: giving a voicemail plan (with 0 messages) moves this part from 0.36 to -1.87 and the predicted risk from 23% to 3%; by state, the part contributes -1.34 in Vermont (risk 5%) and 1.42 in Washington (risk 46%) against 0.36 in the held state. Voicemail-plan holders churn at 7.4% in training against 16.6% without the plan. Fixing the part at its mean lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.903. The full linear formula is attached as evidence (within 0.0039).
ann_89.proposed: This part adds a fixed amount for each input: a voice-mail plan lowers the predicted chance, some states raise or lower it, and higher international and daytime charges raise it steadily.

ann_90.original: Service-call churn trigger: the unit switches on once a customer has made several customer-service calls, sooner when day-time usage is low and later when it is high, and while it is on it raises the model's churn score (directly through its edge to the output and again through state11ServiceGate, which it feeds). Self-probe on the typical customer (the held case), sweeping service calls: the unit is 0.00 at 2 calls, 0.16 at 3 and 0.67 at 4, and in the whole model the predicted risk goes from 22% at 2 calls to 67% at 4 and 93% at 5. With low day usage (100 day minutes, 17 dollars day charge) it is already 0.35 at 2 calls; with heavy day usage (280 minutes, 47.6 dollars) it is 0.00 at 4 calls and 0.32 at 5. On the training split it acts on 890 of 4000 customers, adding 1.44 to the score on average through this part for those customers; their churn rate is 20.7% against 12.3% for the rest. Of the 318 customers with 4 or more service calls it acts on 303; the other 587 customers it acts on have fewer than 4 calls (mostly low day usage), and their churn rate is only 5.8%. Switching this part off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.839. Its closed form (attached) reproduces the unit to within 0.0019.
ann_90.proposed: This part switches on once a customer makes several calls to customer service, sooner when daytime use is low, and then raises the predicted chance in an uneven way.

ann_91.original: Service-call relay with a Hawaii exception: the unit takes the serviceCallsLowDay signal, adds a further push from the number of service calls, and passes it to the output and (as a brake) to intlPlanGate; a large negative weight on the Hawaii indicator holds it off for customers in Hawaii. Self-probe, sweeping service calls on the typical customer: the unit is 0.00 at 3 calls and 0.58 at 4, rising to 3.90 at 9 calls. The same sweep in Hawaii leaves it at 0.00 at 9 calls, and the whole-model predicted risk at 9 calls is 92% in Hawaii against above 99% in the held state (Hawaii also has its own negative direct term, in directTerms). On the training split it acts on 517 customers, 502 of whom also have serviceCallsLowDay on, adding 1.08 to the score on average through this part; their churn rate is 32.9%. It is on for 0 of the 73 training customers in Hawaii. Switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.907. Closed form attached (within 0.003).
ann_91.proposed: This part passes on the service-call signal and adds to it in an uneven way as calls mount, while being in Hawaii holds it back.

ann_92.original: International-plan churn push: the unit is on for customers with the international plan and raises their churn score; the service-call relay (state11ServiceGate) feeds it with a negative weight, so the push shrinks as service calls mount. It also feeds state17Gate and one hinge of heavyUsageNoVmail, both negatively (see serviceIntlUsageCore). Self-probe on the typical customer: turning the international plan on moves the unit from 0.00 to 1.15 and the whole-model predicted risk from 23% to 79%. With the plan, going from 3 to 9 service calls lowers the unit from 1.15 to 0.34 while state11ServiceGate rises to 3.90; the predicted risk still rises (to above 99%) because the service-call route adds more than this unit loses. On the training split it acts on 380 of the 380 plan holders (a share of 100%) and on 0 customers without the plan; for the plan holders it adds 2.33 to the score on average through this part, and their churn rate is 42.4% against 11.2% without the plan. Switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.850. Closed form attached (within 0.0002).
ann_92.proposed: This part switches on for customers with an international plan and raises their predicted chance, more so in Connecticut.

ann_93.original: Small background offset with a Kentucky boost: the unit is on for 3626 of 4000 training customers and lowers the churn score slightly; it is larger in Kentucky, and the international-plan gate switches it off for most plan holders. Self-probe on the typical customer: it contributes -0.022 to the score without the international plan and 0.000 with it; in Kentucky it contributes -0.265 without the plan and -0.218 with it. On the training split it is off for 374 customers, 374 of whom have intlPlanGate on; it stays on for 6 of the 380 international-plan holders, 1 of them outside Kentucky. For the 81 Kentucky customers it adds -0.262 on average through this part. It barely matters for ranking: switching it off changes the training AUC from 0.9178 to 0.9175 and the mean predicted risk by -0.0039. Closed form attached (within 0.0025).
ann_93.proposed: This small part lowers the predicted chance for customers in Kentucky.

ann_94.original: Heavy-usage churn trigger: the unit switches on when day-time minutes (helped by evening and night charges) are high, and adds a large churn push that grows with usage; voicemail messages raise the threshold, and the international-plan gate lowers one of its two hinges. Self-probe, sweeping day minutes on the typical customer (no voicemail, day charge held at its typical value): the unit is 0.00 at 225 minutes and 0.70 at 250, and the whole-model predicted risk goes from 23% to 62% and then 98% at 300 minutes. With a voicemail plan and 30 messages the unit is 0.00 at 275 minutes and 0.55 at 300. At 275 minutes, adding the international plan lowers the unit from 1.42 to 1.02. On the training split it acts on 711 customers, adding 2.28 to the score on average through this part; their churn rate is 37.7% against 9.1% for the rest. It acts on 55 of the 1060 customers with voicemail messages and on 656 of the 2940 without. Switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.799, the largest loss of any leaf. Closed form attached (within 0.0037).
ann_94.proposed: This part switches on for heavy daytime use, from about 238 minutes (between 193 minutes and 289 minutes for different customers), and then raises the predicted chance in an uneven way; a high evening charge makes the rise steeper.

ann_95.original: Extra per-state offsets on top of the direct state terms: each unit reads one or a few state indicators, so the part adds the same small baseline for most states and moves the score for customers in a few. Self-probe, sweeping the state of the typical customer: the part contributes 0.008 in the held state (West Virginia) but -2.14 in Arkansas, where the predicted risk falls to 3% from 23%; North Dakota (-0.48) and South Carolina (-0.38) get smaller reductions, Maine (0.11) and Idaho (0.10) small increases, and Massachusetts (-0.022), Mississippi (-0.020) and Texas (0.006) almost no change. The Arkansas offset looks fitted to 78 training customers: their churn rate is 17.9%, not below the 14.1% of the rest, yet their mean predicted risk is 17% against 37%. The other regimes are also small: North Dakota 68, South Carolina 66, Maine 86 and Idaho 98 training customers, and 258 in Massachusetts, Mississippi and Texas together. In the Maine chain, the two units after the Maine unit are on for 0 training customers, so the Idaho unit works on its own input. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.919. Closed form attached (within 0.033).
ann_95.proposed: This part adds a further fixed adjustment for a handful of states, mostly lowering the predicted chance.

ann_96.original: Two small usage units. The voicemail-message unit raises the churn score with each message, adding to the direct message edge: for an otherwise typical customer with a voicemail plan, this part contributes -0.06 at 0 messages and 0.55 at 50, and in the whole model the predicted risk goes from 3% to 28%. The night-charge unit turns on above a low night charge (0.00 at 6 dollars, 0.15 at 8), and its rise is offset by the negative direct night-charge edge: the whole-model predicted risk is 24% at 6 dollars and 23% at 14 dollars (it moves at 16 dollars, 31%, through heavyUsageNoVmail, not this part). The night unit is on for 2965 training customers. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.915. Closed form attached (within 0.0023).
ann_96.proposed: This part raises the predicted chance steadily with more voice-mail messages, and with the night-time charge once it passes about 7.57 US dollars.

ann_97.original: Three churn routes, chained rather than independent. Route one is many customer-service calls (serviceCallsLowDay, relayed by state11ServiceGate); route two is the international plan (intlPlanGate); route three is heavy usage (heavyUsageNoVmail); state17Gate is a small offset. The routes are linked in series: state11ServiceGate feeds intlPlanGate with a negative weight, and intlPlanGate feeds state17Gate and one hinge of heavyUsageNoVmail with negative weights, so when one route is already on, a second route adds less than it would alone. Self-probe on the typical customer: with 1 service call, the international plan moves the score from -1.19 to 1.31; 5 calls without the plan give 2.61; both together give 4.56, less than the two changes added, because intlPlanGate falls from 1.15 to 0.89 once the service-call relay is on. Likewise at 275 day minutes the plan lowers heavyUsageNoVmail from 1.42 to 1.02. On the training split 1778 customers have at least one of the three route units on (serviceCallsLowDay, intlPlanGate or heavyUsageNoVmail); their churn rate is 28.9% against 2.3% for the 2222 customers with none of them on. Switching the whole core off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.629, the largest loss of any part.
ann_97.proposed: This part holds the three churn routes: many calls to customer service, an international plan and heavy daytime use each switch on a part for a group of customers and raise the predicted chance.

ann_98.original: Root: the churn score is the sum of directTerms, serviceIntlUsageCore, stateBumps and vmailNightUnits plus the output bias, passed through the sigmoid; the annotated model reproduces the network to within 4.4e-16 on the training split. In domain terms the model predicts churn through three routes (many customer-service calls, the international plan, heavy usage), with the voicemail plan and a handful of states shifting the baseline. Self-probe: the training customers with none of the three route units on (2222 of them) get a mean predicted risk of 20% and churn at 2.3%, while the 1778 with at least one on get 58% and churn at 28.9%; for a constructed typical customer, 5 service calls and the international plan together raise the predicted risk from 23% to 99%. The core carries most of the ranking: the training AUC is 0.918 with every part, 0.629 without the core, 0.903 with directTerms fixed at its mean, 0.919 without stateBumps and 0.915 without vmailNightUnits. The predicted risks run high: the mean predicted risk on the training split is 37% against an observed churn rate of 14.1%, so the model ranks customers well but its risks are not calibrated probabilities.
ann_98.proposed: The model adds up four parts: three churn routes (many calls to customer service, an international plan and heavy daytime use), a set of plan, state and charge terms, extra state adjustments, and a small voice-mail and night-time part. For a typical customer an international plan raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 23% to about 79%, while a voice-mail plan and some states lower it.

parts.name: churnModel
parts.original_hypothesis: Root: the churn score is the sum of directTerms, serviceIntlUsageCore, stateBumps and vmailNightUnits plus the output bias, passed through the sigmoid; the annotated model reproduces the network to within 4.4e-16 on the training split. In domain terms the model predicts churn through three routes (many customer-service calls, the international plan, heavy usage), with the voicemail plan and a handful of states shifting the baseline. Self-probe: the training customers with none of the three route units on (2222 of them) get a mean predicted risk of 20% and churn at 2.3%, while the 1778 with at least one on get 58% and churn at 28.9%; for a constructed typical customer, 5 service calls and the international plan together raise the predicted risk from 23% to 99%. The core carries most of the ranking: the training AUC is 0.918 with every part, 0.629 without the core, 0.903 with directTerms fixed at its mean, 0.919 without stateBumps and 0.915 without vmailNightUnits. The predicted risks run high: the mean predicted risk on the training split is 37% against an observed churn rate of 14.1%, so the model ranks customers well but its risks are not calibrated probabilities.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: serviceIntlUsageCore
parts.original_hypothesis: Three churn routes, chained rather than independent. Route one is many customer-service calls (serviceCallsLowDay, relayed by state11ServiceGate); route two is the international plan (intlPlanGate); route three is heavy usage (heavyUsageNoVmail); state17Gate is a small offset. The routes are linked in series: state11ServiceGate feeds intlPlanGate with a negative weight, and intlPlanGate feeds state17Gate and one hinge of heavyUsageNoVmail with negative weights, so when one route is already on, a second route adds less than it would alone. Self-probe on the typical customer: with 1 service call, the international plan moves the score from -1.19 to 1.31; 5 calls without the plan give 2.61; both together give 4.56, less than the two changes added, because intlPlanGate falls from 1.15 to 0.89 once the service-call relay is on. Likewise at 275 day minutes the plan lowers heavyUsageNoVmail from 1.42 to 1.02. On the training split 1778 customers have at least one of the three route units on (serviceCallsLowDay, intlPlanGate or heavyUsageNoVmail); their churn rate is 28.9% against 2.3% for the 2222 customers with none of them on. Switching the whole core off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.629, the largest loss of any part.
variables: number of calls to customer service

parts.name: directTerms
parts.original_hypothesis: The direct edges form a linear score added to the output. The largest terms, per standard deviation of the input and through each input's own edge: voice mail plan -0.99, number of voicemail messages 0.51, Vermont -0.24, Hawaii -0.17, international charge 0.16, Washington 0.14 and day charge 0.13. The direct customer-service-call edge is small (-0.09): the service-call effect comes through the gates in serviceIntlUsageCore. Self-probe on the typical customer: giving a voicemail plan (with 0 messages) moves this part from 0.36 to -1.87 and the predicted risk from 23% to 3%; by state, the part contributes -1.34 in Vermont (risk 5%) and 1.42 in Washington (risk 46%) against 0.36 in the held state. Voicemail-plan holders churn at 7.4% in training against 16.6% without the plan. Fixing the part at its mean lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.903. The full linear formula is attached as evidence (within 0.0039).

parts.original_hypothesis: International-plan churn push: the unit is on for customers with the international plan and raises their churn score; the service-call relay (state11ServiceGate) feeds it with a negative weight, so the push shrinks as service calls mount. It also feeds state17Gate and one hinge of heavyUsageNoVmail, both negatively (see serviceIntlUsageCore). Self-probe on the typical customer: turning the international plan on moves the unit from 0.00 to 1.15 and the whole-model predicted risk from 23% to 79%. With the plan, going from 3 to 9 service calls lowers the unit from 1.15 to 0.34 while state11ServiceGate rises to 3.90; the predicted risk still rises (to above 99%) because the service-call route adds more than this unit loses. On the training split it acts on 380 of the 380 plan holders (a share of 100%) and on 0 customers without the plan; for the plan holders it adds 2.33 to the score on average through this part, and their churn rate is 42.4% against 11.2% without the plan. Switching it off lowers the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.850. Closed form attached (within 0.0002).

parts.name: stateBumps
parts.original_hypothesis: Extra per-state offsets on top of the direct state terms: each unit reads one or a few state indicators, so the part adds the same small baseline for most states and moves the score for customers in a few. Self-probe, sweeping the state of the typical customer: the part contributes 0.008 in the held state (West Virginia) but -2.14 in Arkansas, where the predicted risk falls to 3% from 23%; North Dakota (-0.48) and South Carolina (-0.38) get smaller reductions, Maine (0.11) and Idaho (0.10) small increases, and Massachusetts (-0.022), Mississippi (-0.020) and Texas (0.006) almost no change. The Arkansas offset looks fitted to 78 training customers: their churn rate is 17.9%, not below the 14.1% of the rest, yet their mean predicted risk is 17% against 37%. The other regimes are also small: North Dakota 68, South Carolina 66, Maine 86 and Idaho 98 training customers, and 258 in Massachusetts, Mississippi and Texas together. In the Maine chain, the two units after the Maine unit are on for 0 training customers, so the Idaho unit works on its own input. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.919. Closed form attached (within 0.033).

parts.name: vmailNightUnits
parts.original_hypothesis: Two small usage units. The voicemail-message unit raises the churn score with each message, adding to the direct message edge: for an otherwise typical customer with a voicemail plan, this part contributes -0.06 at 0 messages and 0.55 at 50, and in the whole model the predicted risk goes from 3% to 28%. The night-charge unit turns on above a low night charge (0.00 at 6 dollars, 0.15 at 8), and its rise is offset by the negative direct night-charge edge: the whole-model predicted risk is 24% at 6 dollars and 23% at 14 dollars (it moves at 16 dollars, 31%, through heavyUsageNoVmail, not this part). The night unit is on for 2965 training customers. Switching the part off changes the training AUC from 0.918 to 0.915. Closed form attached (within 0.0023).

parts.name: state17Gate
parts.original_hypothesis: Small background offset with a Kentucky boost: the unit is on for 3626 of 4000 training customers and lowers the churn score slightly; it is larger in Kentucky, and the international-plan gate switches it off for most plan holders. Self-probe on the typical customer: it contributes -0.022 to the score without the international plan and 0.000 with it; in Kentucky it contributes -0.265 without the plan and -0.218 with it. On the training split it is off for 374 customers, 374 of whom have intlPlanGate on; it stays on for 6 of the 380 international-plan holders, 1 of them outside Kentucky. For the 81 Kentucky customers it adds -0.262 on average through this part. It barely matters for ranking: switching it off changes the training AUC from 0.9178 to 0.9175 and the mean predicted risk by -0.0039. Closed form attached (within 0.0025).

reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

For a typical customer it acts on, it clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 19% without this part to about 44% with it.
In the training data, 184 of these 890 customers had churn.

A higher total daytime minutes clearly raises the predicted chance that a customer leaves, and even more so if customer-service calls is at or below 1 calls (in an uneven way for patients with customer-service calls at or below 1 calls): for a typical customer, total daytime minutes going from 112 minutes to 249 minutes moves the predicted chance that a customer leaves from about 20% to about 64% if customer-service calls is at or below 1 calls, and from about 24% to about 61% if customer-service calls is above 1 calls.

summary.text: For a typical customer, the model gives a clearly higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer has an international plan (about 79%) than if the customer has no international plan (about 23%).

For a typical customer, the model gives a higher predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in Washington (about 46%) than if state is something other than Alabama, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Arkansas, Maine, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oklahoma, California, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, Connecticut, Florida (about 23%) (on the training data only).

For a typical customer, the model gives a lower predicted chance that a customer leaves if the customer is in Arkansas (about 3%) than if state is something other than Alabama, Hawaii, Idaho, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Massachusetts, Arkansas, Maine, Minnesota, Missouri, Mississippi, Montana, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, Oklahoma, California, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, Vermont, Washington, Wisconsin, Connecticut, Florida (about 23%) (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, total daytime charge adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 37.65 US dollars (between 30.48 and 41.83 US dollars for different customers) (for 2363 of the 4000 training customers it already changes below that): for a typical such customer, going from 0.00 US dollars to 46.09 US dollars moves it from about 23% to about 91%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, total daytime minutes clearly adds to the predicted chance that a customer leaves once it rises above about 238 minutes (between 193 and 289 minutes for different customers) (for 1840 of the 4000 training customers it already changes below that): for a typical such customer, going from 0 minutes to 271 minutes moves it from about 23% to about 88%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way.

The model ignores account length, area code, total daytime calls and total international calls; it does not read total international minutes and total night-time minutes itself (it reads inputs the data ties to them).
